title: Pale at the Front: The Politics of Showing Up
sources: ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T, 2016), RS political-military command structure
Balkan Battlegrounds, Vol. I (CIA, 2002), VRS corps organisation and the Posavina corridor
content:
For Republika Srpska's leadership the front visit was a transaction in loyalty, a currency long campaigns and thin rations steadily spent. The VRS soldier held his ground, but the political authority at Pale knew that holding was not the same as believing, and that a president seen among the troops bought something a directive could not. Where to be seen — the Posavina corridor under constant pressure, the Sarajevo siege lines of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, or the Drina Corps holding the east — was itself a statement about which front Pale judged most fragile, and which it could afford to leave to its officers.

The ICTY record of the RS command describes a political leadership tightly entwined with its generals, where the line between civilian authority and military direction was deliberately thin. In that structure a visit was never neutral. Radovan Karadžić's appearances at the front projected the unity of the project; they also exposed the leadership to the same risk the troops carried, and to the international scrutiny that followed the Bosnian Serb side everywhere by 1993. To stay at Pale, pleading the demands of governance, kept the leadership safe and the diplomacy centralised, but let the soldier wonder whether his sacrifice registered above him.

The gesture cuts both ways. To tour the corridor was to honour the men holding the thread that kept the western Serb-held territories connected to Serbia, while drawing attention to how thin that thread was. To walk the siege lines around Sarajevo was to associate the leadership openly with the most internationally damning front. To visit the Drina was to reassure the east at the cost of signalling priority away from the corridor. None of it added ground; all of it shaped how the rank and file read the worth Pale placed on their war.

This is a recurring leadership choice, not a sourced single trip, and the Codex reflects the most recent one. It belongs to the register of morale and cohesion, not operations — the question Pale faced was whether presence would steady a strained army or merely advertise the strain. A visit could harden resolve; it could equally look like a leadership inspecting a war it was no longer sure it controlled.
